title: Arrays
summary: Index access is O(1); a middle insert shifts the tail.

parts.rule: Reach element i with one address calculation. That is the contract an array keeps. Shifting a middle slot forces every later element to move, so that update is linear in the tail length.
parts.why: Interviews ask you to name the shape before you write a loop. When the prompt needs random jumps into a buffer, an array matches the cost story. When the prompt keeps splicing in the middle of a live chain of nodes, the same shape becomes expensive. Saying the cost out loud shows you are choosing on purpose, not from habit.
parts.example: SAMPLE: you hold ten integers in a contiguous buffer and the interviewer asks for the value at index 7. You compute base plus seven widths and return it in constant time. Later they ask you to insert a value at index 2. You slide indices 2 through 9 one slot right, then write the new value. That slide is the O(n) part you must name.
parts.use: Pick an array when the work is mostly indexed reads and writes, when appends dominate and middle edits are rare, or when a later algorithm needs a dense ordered view for a binary search. Dynamic growth is fine if you can accept occasional full copies when the buffer doubles.
parts.refuse: Refuse an array when the hot path is insert or delete in the middle of a long sequence and you already hold a handle to the place you change. Refuse it when the size is unknown and every growth copy would dominate the budget you just estimated. Prefer a linked structure or a deque when both ends move and the middle almost never needs an index.

body:
Rule. Reach element i with one address calculation. That is the contract an array keeps. Shifting a middle slot forces every later element to move, so that update is linear in the tail length.

Why it matters. Interviews ask you to name the shape before you write a loop. When the prompt needs random jumps into a buffer, an array matches the cost story. When the prompt keeps splicing in the middle of a live chain of nodes, the same shape becomes expensive. Saying the cost out loud shows you are choosing on purpose, not from habit.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: you hold ten integers in a contiguous buffer and the interviewer asks for the value at index 7. You compute base plus seven widths and return it in constant time. Later they ask you to insert a value at index 2. You slide indices 2 through 9 one slot right, then write the new value. That slide is the O(n) part you must name.

When to use. Pick an array when the work is mostly indexed reads and writes, when appends dominate and middle edits are rare, or when a later algorithm needs a dense ordered view for a binary search. Dynamic growth is fine if you can accept occasional full copies when the buffer doubles.

When to refuse. Refuse an array when the hot path is insert or delete in the middle of a long sequence and you already hold a handle to the place you change. Refuse it when the size is unknown and every growth copy would dominate the budget you just estimated. Prefer a linked structure or a deque when both ends move and the middle almost never needs an index.

Recall checkpoint 1: say the cost in one sentence, name the competing shape, and restate the refuse rule in your own words before you leave this SAMPLE lesson.
